utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently our screens are empty. We have nothing on our screens. Oh, it's better now. It's fine now. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mr. Demirdjian, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On this Monday, the 14th of February, 2005, 183rd day of hearings, I bid good afternoon to the Prosecution, the Defence, the two accused, as well as all the personnel in this courtroom, be they inside or outside the courtroom. Before beginning hearing the witness, there are several small problems that we need to deal with. First of all, I wish to inform the parties that I was informed by the President of this Tribunal of the possibility that we will have to work on Friday afternoon. As you know, in the interest of good management and to allow both the Prosecution and the Defence to prepare well for the next week of hearings, it was decided up to now that we would not sit on Monday morning or Friday afternoon. However, we know that the Defence needs to meet their witnesses and we know the difficult conditions under which they are working, because you told us quite recently that you would have -- you had to work very late at night and to have documents copied during the night to disclose to the Prosecution, which illustrate the difficulties you are encountering. And to give you the Friday afternoon and the Monday morning time to prepare was, we felt, a good solution, which allowed us to proceed smoothly. However, the President has explained to me that we have three courtrooms and that currently there are three trials on going -- six trials, which means that for this reason we need to sit on Fridays afternoons. Aware of this difficulty, I informed the Registrar; however, they maintain their position, which is that as of the 1st of March, we will have to sit on Friday's afternoon. We take note of this, and if they have -- if anyone has any problems, I advise them to contact the President of the Tribunal or the Registrar. Personally, I feel that to work for five consecutive days is already a heavy burden, particularly as we are sitting without any breaks since December 2003. If this measure can apply to very short trials, in the case of longer trials like this one perhaps it would be appropriate to reduce the number of working days, because, as far as I know, in no country in the world do we have five consecutive sittings, five consecutive days of sitting, for months on end. And if anyone would like to comment on this, I would be glad to give them the floor. That was by way of information for both parties. I also wish to inform the parties about something that we Judges have discussed. In the month of April, there is a holiday, that is, Friday, the 29th of April. Like last year, we will have a break in the month of April, and it will start from Monday, the 25th of April going through until Friday, the 29th. This will certainly be of interest to the Defence of General Kubura because at that time we will be having the Defence witnesses for General Kubura. So I wish to inform them of this so that they can take note of it and act accordingly. I now move on to another subject, but I should like to discuss it in private session. Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to deal with the question of the documents. And I give the floor to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence proposals -- proposes the following documents, that is, number 3, 1717; number 4, 1724; and number 22, 1775, to be marked for identification as they only exist in B/C/S. We should like to tender as exhibits documents under number 7, 1726; number 9, 1727; number 10, 1735; number 11, 1737; number 13, 1742; number 14, 0804; number 17, 0859; number 18, 0874; number 20, 0909. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objections, Mr. President. I would ask before the next witness is brought into the courtroom my co-counsel has a few issues he'd like to raise with the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, will you please do your duty and give us final numbers for these documents to be marked for identification first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following documents are being marked for identification. I will give the numbers in English to avoid any errors. [In English] DH177 [sic], marked for identification; DH1724, marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop for a moment. There's a mistake. At the outset. Line 15, it's -- it's not 177. It's 1717. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next document is DH1726, English version DH1726/E. DH1727, its English translation DH1727/E. The Registry notes that DH1735 is already an exhibit. DH1737 with its English translation, DH1737/E. 1742, DH1742, with its English translation, DH1742/E. DH804, its English translation, DH804/E. DH1 -- sorry, 859, English translation DH859/E. The DH874, its English translation, DH874/E. DH909, with its English translation, DH909/E. Eventually the DH1775, marked for identification only. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I turn to the Prosecution, who would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good afternoon, Mr. President. There are a few points I would like to raise are the following: The first one, if the Defence, I take it, in closed session or private session could tell us the order of the witnesses -- or rather, the -- I think the last witness on Friday hasn't been yet confirmed or even told the name. And second, also to confirm the witness for Thursday. The other point though, Mr. President, is somewhat related to what you told us about the burden of the Defence to conduct their case, to disclose documents and so on, and so the related burden on the Prosecution. Again, for today's witness we have received only this morning 42 documents and 18 of them have not been translated into English, so are in B/C/S. Something similar occurred last week. I believe it was the BH military attache in the US, Mr. Husic, and there again we had out of 64 documents only 30 -- or 30 were only in B/C/S. And, Your Honours, that's really difficult for us to -- to prepare. Of course, we -- we do have language assistants, but not the same day the witness is -- is coming to testify. If these documents are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disclosed a week before, it's -- it's really easier for us, and not the same day. If it's only about one or two documents the same day or the night before, that's really fine. We can deal with that. But 30 new, untranslated documents, that's -- that's difficult. And we, you know, reserve our right to recall these witnesses once we have received the English translations and assessed that we have to -- to ask a few questions to these witnesses. So we would make an assessment then whether we need to recall these witnesses, and obviously that's a -- a issue about resources and timing, which -- which we don't want to do. But I just wanted -- wanted to inform Your Honours about this point. And just to -- to make it clear, it's about disclosure and -- and translation, and we have absolutely no objections to the Defence bringing in new documents. That's their right. We know exactly the way it is. But it's sort of the untimely disclosure of untranslated documents in this case. The next point is a little bit related. That's the insufficiency of the 65 ter summaries. We had a number of witnesses who really went beyond these summaries. And again, it's very difficult for us to prepare then these witnesses. You might recall I think last week or the week before a witness -- an international witness talked about a secret source, and I believe in other Trial Chambers the Defence team would inform the Prosecution orally, "This witness has done something -- told us something new," perhaps proofing notes, whatever. But if the Defence could -- could tell us in advance, you know, what's coming, that would be very helpful, if it goes beyond the 65 ter summaries. That's the points I wanted to raise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to the Defence. But before I do that, I should like to make two remarks. This is a repeating problem that we are encountering. So the Prosecution is raising two problems. The first is the summaries of witnesses are highly concise; that is, the list, one can say. And the Prosecution notices that sometimes the Defence addresses points that are not contained in the summaries. And the Prosecution tell us that they are encountering difficulties because they were unable to prepare properly. At this stage, without making any judgement, I would like to say in my own name that the witness summaries were far more detailed when the Prosecution provided those summaries than the Defence summaries, which are highly -- summary, and in those conditions it is very difficult for the Prosecution to prepare. So I am asking you to respond regarding this matter, which is not being raised for the first time. If I were to review the transcripts, it is at least the fifth time that the Prosecution is raising this problem. The second problem which the Defence will certainly clarify for us, and it follows on to what has just been said, that this -- the time needed to prepare for witnesses, that this morning they received dozens of documents, a large portion of which have not been translated, which means that the Prosecution, in spite of the vast resources it has at its disposal, cannot prepare properly for the cross-examination because the documents are in B/C/S, and this is a true problem. The Chamber through me would like to know why the Defence did not consider it useful to have those documents translated before, or maybe they found those documents at the last moment, which could be an explanation, or you certainly must have encountered difficulties and could you let us know what those were. In view of the fact that the Prosecution has raised a certain number of problems and it is your duty to respond, I give the floor - I don't know whom - to Mr. Bourgon. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, I will respond to the points raised by my learned friend from the Prosecution and in the same order in which he raised them. First of all, my learned friend from the Prosecution spoke about the witness of last Friday. Last Friday's witness I discussed with one of the officials from the Prosecution to explain that this witness is a witness who was substituted for another witness who could not come. I myself didn't have the name of this witness. He was a technical witness who will come to speak about distances and what one could see with binoculars. And I informed my colleague of this, saying that as soon as I have the name of this witness, I will be able to communicate it to him. And I can tell him today the name of that person. The witness who should have testified this week Friday -- I think I need to read the name in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, I would like to ask you to stand up, because you have to take the solemn declaration. Can you please give me your first name, your last name, the date of birth, and the place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mladen Veseljak. I was born on 28 May 1952 in Zenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you a member of any bar or associations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a member of the Regional Bar of Zenica in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, were you employed? Did you work? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in 1992. Up to 12 October, I worked as the director of personnel department in an export company, and after that I was a judge of the military district court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international tribunal or a national court about the developments that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have testified before this Tribunal, and if my memory serves me well, it was in 1998, at the beginning of that year, in the Blaskic case, and I was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can you please read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I do it like this? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence lawyers, I would like to provide you with some information about your testimony. However, as a former judge and as an attorney-at-law, I'm sure that you understand the procedure very well. You're here to answer questions put to you by the Defence team of the General -- of General Hadzihasanovic, whom you have already met in preparation of your testimony. They have informed us that they will need about an hour and a half for their examination-in-chief. After that, the Defence team of General Kubura, who are seated on my right, will also be given the floor to put some questions to you if they so wish. We are here practicing the kind of procedure which is a combination of the common law and German law, but let me tell you that the questions put to you by the Defence should not be leading, should be neutral in their nature. If they put to you a question that might appear leading, the Prosecution will certainly object. After the examination-in-chief, the representatives of the Prosecution, seated on your right, will have the right to cross-examine you; however, their questions may be leading. They may be formulated in such a way that sometimes it will suffice for you to answer either by "yes" or "no." They are allowed to put such questions to you. At the end of that stage, the Defence may have some additional questions for you that will be linked with the questions put to you during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the cross-examination. The Defence will certainly have some documents to show you. They will ask you whether you are familiar with these documents, whether you know something about them, and so on and so forth. The three Judges, who are in front of you, can ask you questions at any moment; however, for the convenience sake and to allow the Defence to evaluate the entirety of your testimony, the Judges prefer to wait until the end to put their questions to you. Whenever the Judges ask you questions, this is with the sole goal in mind, and that is to search for the truth. That is why we will ask you questions either to clarify some of the answers that you provided to the questions put to you by the two sides or if the Judges deem that none of the parties has asked you some important questions that are important and that will help the Judges to arrive at the truth. At the end of that stage, after the Judges' questions, both the Defence and the Prosecution will have the right to ask you questions arising from the Judges' questions. If at any moment a question appears too complicated to you, you have the right to ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it; however, since you yourself are an attorney-at-law, I believe that you will not have any problems with any of the questions. I have to remind you of two other things that appear in our Rules of Procedure, and I'm doing this just to remind you of them, although we have never been in the position to apply those Rules. You have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you are not to -- to give us false testimony. And the second technical question is that when a question is put to the witness, the witness may refuse to answer that question if he believes that the answer may one day be used against him or incriminate him. And in that case, a very exceptional case that we have not seen so far, in this very hypothetical case the Chamber may compel the witness to answer such questions; however, the Chamber will guarantee the witness immunity. And this is in very general outlines how your testimony is going to proceed. If at any moment you encounter a difficult in your testimony, you can always ask for our help. For example, if your health does not allow for the correct answer or if you're tired. Let me just tell you one more thing for technical reasons and to allow you to take a short rest, we will have a break every hour and a half. Since we started at quarter past 2.00, we will have our first break at quarter to 4.00 for 20 minutes and then we will proceed. If everything goes well, which I fully believe that it will, your testimony should end today. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence, who are going to start their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that by occupation you are an attorney-at-law. Will you tell us your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I graduated at the Faculty of Law at the university in Sarajevo in 1976. After that, I took all the other examinations prescribed by our legal system to be able to act as an attorney, so I took the judicial examination and later the exam for attorneys-at-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, for how many years were you a judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Just under 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What cases did you deal with as a judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Always criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Colleague, I would now like to make an observation that I omitted to do at the beginning. As what we are saying needs to be interpreted for Their Honours to be able to follow, would you please wait a few seconds for my question to be translated before answering it. Tell me, please, what was the ethnic composition of the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It was Bosnian, which means there were Bosniak, Croats, and I was a Serb. Among the judges, of course. Roughly the composition reflected -- among the judges, reflected the same composition as the rest of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, was there any inequality or any discrimination towards colleagues with different ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, Mr. Veseljak: Your district military court in Zenica in those days, was it part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It was not then nor ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. My colleague tells me that in French "district military court" was translated as "a cantonal court." I think the word should be "district" because cantonal courts were established after the war only, so I think it is advisable to have the same term used in both languages. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you did not belong to the army nor were you under its wing, what kind of relationships existed between the district military court and the 3rd Corps of the BH army or any other military units of the BH army in those days?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Professional relationships only; that is to say, certain elements of the BH army or the corps. And I am referring to the Security Services, the military police. They serviced or carried out the instructions of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, colleague, did the 3rd Corps manifest its interest in maintaining good cooperation with the district military court and were there any pressures to that effect or were those relationships based on the law and the position of the court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Naturally the corps did have an interest in the proper functioning of the district military court, which I thought then and still think was only normal. There were literally no pressures, not even suggestions, on the part of the corps command as to how we should work or what we should do. If I may say this in this courtroom, I remember an event or a meeting, a courtesy meeting -- actually, that was the only occasion when I actually saw the gentleman who is on trial here today, Mr. Hadzihasanovic. It took place shortly after the formation of the corps when all of us judges of the district military courts and the military prosecutor and his deputies were invited to meet Mr. Hadzihasanovic. This was the only direct contact we had. And as it was the only one, I remember it well. Mr. Hadzihasanovic said first that he apologised for not coming to see us but, rather, invited us to come and see him because he had so much to do that he couldn't leave his command. He wanted to meet us, and he wanted to ask us to do our utmost to speed up our criminal proceedings as much as possible because that was in the interests of all of us and our goal, which was to defend us and form a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, tell me, please: On what bases did the judges of the district military court operate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: On the basis of the Law on Criminal Procedure taken over from the former SFRY and on the basis of certain amendments made to it through decrees with the effect of law in amending that Law on Criminal Procedure. So the same laws were applied as were used by all the other courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who decided on appeal in relation to your rulings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Two courts of a higher level. As a district military court, we were responsible for all criminal acts committed by military personnel. Sometimes we judged individually. In some cases there were one or -- were several judges, and in the most -- in the gravest cases, there were three judges. In the first case, the appeals court in Zenica was responsible for appeals against our rulings when we ruled individually.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to district military courts in the judicial system of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there any other judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: There were courts that we called regular courts. Now they're known as municipal courts. Earlier they were known as basic courts, higher courts, and the supreme court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the difference between basic and higher courts as regular courts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Only in terms of the level of competencies. If we're talking about crimes, then basic courts would try crimes envisaging sentences up to ten years, and higher courts covered crimes for which sentences were envisaged above ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember and tell us how many regular courts there were in the territory covered by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Actually, I'm not quite certain regarding the territory covered by the 3rd Corps, but I think there was the higher court in Zenica in that area, the municipal court in Zenica, the municipal court in Travnik, the municipal court in Kakanj, I think in Zavidovici, I think even in Maglaj. There were five or six. There may even have been up to eight municipal courts and one higher court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What persons were tried by regular courts in criminal cases?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Civilians, and some military persons if they were co-perpetrators in crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that district military courts tried military personnel. Tell me first how many district military courts there were in the area of Central Bosnia, that is, the area of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: There were two; one in Zenica and one in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What acts were they responsible for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: They were responsible for all criminal acts committed by military personnel. As for civilians, a certain number of criminal offences, mostly covered by two chapters of the Criminal Code. There were -- one set were crimes against the social order, and the other set were crimes against the armed forces. Should there be dispute over competencies, if a civilian was to be tried simultaneously for a criminal offence within the competence of the district military court and another offence within the competence of the civilian court, in that case both -- the person would be tried for both offences in the military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm informed by my colleague that the answer you gave may be not quite precise, on page 33, line 16, so I'll ask you the question once again. Will you tell me, please, what persons were regular courts -- had jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Over civilians and also military personnel if they were co-perpetrators with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that you tried in accordance with the procedure laid down by the Law on Criminal Procedure taken over from the former SFRY and applied as the republican law. Tell me whether the criminal proceedings in regular courts were conducted in accordance with the same law or in some different manner in those courts.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: There was no difference. We were guided by the same law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to responsibility of persons for acts committed within our system and pursuant to the law, were there any other bodies which would decide about the responsibility of individuals?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were bodies that established and ruled certain disciplinary measures for disciplinary offences. Then there were two-level courts for misdemeanours, and in establishing responsibility and sanctioning those offences, there's what is known as the judicial protection. This is an extraordinary remedy. And only beyond that were there courses -- courts that tried criminal offences as laid down by the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that there were -- there was judicial control of decisions made by magistrate courts. That is why I am asking you, Mr. Veseljak, whether those magistrate courts and those disciplinary bodies were a component part of the judicial system or were they a component part of some other state structure.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I may not have quite understood your question initially. Disciplinary bodies and the system of magistrate courts were never part of the judicial system, and they are not today. Magistrate courts are administrative bodies, and disciplinary bodies are located within other bodies and they have legal jurisdiction to sanction certain disciplinary violations or violations of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Veseljak: In the legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the body that carried out the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The responsible prosecutor exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to certain procedural matters, I should just like to ask you one more thing: Do you have any knowledge, awareness of the existence of any other courts that were not part of the judicial system but were within the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I know that there was a decree with the effect of law on so-called special military courts. I knew and still know the gist of that decree. It prescribed the possibility of forming special military courts exclusively to sanction conduct contrary to the interests of the armed forces and only on condition that serious consequences ensued from that act, as the only sanction that those courts could issue was the death penalty. And there was a corrector which said should that court discover the existence of any mitigating circumstances which would not lead to the death penalty, then the proceedings in those courts would be interrupted and the case diverted to regular military courts. I know that in several military units such courts were formed, but I am not aware of them ever adopting any such decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I will be using some documents with this witness and it is now time for the break, perhaps it would be a good idea to distribute this set of documents so the witness could have a look at the documents to be able to answer my questions more easily. And let me just say that this is the same set of documents that will be used for the witness that appear -- will appear after this witness. So could this binder be given to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please distribute the documents. It is quarter to 4.00. We shall now have the break for 20 to 25 minutes. The witness will be able to rest and also consult the binder. So we will resume at ten past 4.00. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, I'll wait for the accused to arrive. Before I give you the floor, with regard to the translation issue, the Chamber has raised two issues: First of all the issue of documents which are in B/C/S, in the binder you provided, and the Prosecution has not had access to these documents. We believe that at this moment the Prosecution is entitled to request additional time at the end of the examination-in-chief in order to look for the documents that have been provided. As a result of that, the witness may be requested to come back later. It is up to the Prosecution. What does the Prosecution have to say? Do you believe that after the examination-in-chief you will be able to conduct your cross-examination, or would you rather conduct your cross-examination on a different occasion, which would require from the witness to come back to The Hague later? Mr. Waespi.

utterances.text: Well, I haven't heard much of the examination-in-chief yet, so I don't know what the witness is going to say about the heart of our case. But anticipating everything I know about the testimony of the witness, I can certainly start and -- and finish cross-examination today. But once we have received translation of these perhaps 30 B/C/S documents, then we need to reassess. That's perhaps in a week or two weeks. I don't know whether, you know, we need to recall the -- the judge and ask additional questions, but we simply can't say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall wait for the end of the examination-in-chief and then you will advise us as to what you wish to do. As regards the other matter, we can discuss it in the presence of the witness because there is nothing to hide there. We believe that the fact has been mentioned that we have 300 documents that haven't been translated yet, and the Prosecution doesn't have these documents. And taking into account the fact that the Registry will be able to provide us with a translation of these documents by 28 February, we believe that we will be able to have a break next week while the documents are being translated. I'm going to ask the registrar to confirm to us whether all of the documents will indeed be provided to the Prosecution in English and to the Defence in the two languages by the 28th of February, that is, next week. So shall we wait for all of us to have all the documents and to have a break in the proceedings, as suggested by Mr. Bourgon. You can inform us about that later. We shall now continue with the examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, before the break, I asked you who was the authorised Prosecution body. And as far as I could understand you, you said that it was the prosecutor. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the document or the piece of regulation in keeping with our Rules of Criminal Procedure served to start this criminal proceedings or prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It started with the request to instigate investigation or proposal for prosecution where there was no need for the investigation to be carried out. Where investigation was not provided for by the law as is stated in the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Before the criminal proceedings were instituted, which body was in charge of the pre-prosecution proceedings and which body decided whether the collective material gives enough reason to support -- suspect that a crime has been committed and that criminal procedures should be started?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It was always the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When this decision was made by the prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was not heard by the French interpreter. Can you please ask the witness to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, before the beginning of criminal proceedings, what body in keeping with the law on criminal procedure was authorised to manage the pre-trial procedure and to decide whether the collected evidence gives ample grounds to start criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It was always the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, once the prosecutor reached the decision that there is enough grounds to start criminal proceedings, did a military body, a court, or the police have a say in that decision or could they influence that decision?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Nobody could have an impact on the prosecutor's decision of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, can you tell us, please, what authorities did the prosecutor have at the moment when he learnt that there were grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed or when he received a criminal report? What is it that the prosecutor could do? What tools were available to him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The prosecutor could accept this criminal report and file a request with the court to start criminal proceedings. He could decide that there were no grounds for further criminal proceedings. And he could reject such a criminal report. He -- in addition to that, he could request from the police and even from the investigative judge of the competent court to carry out certain pre-trial investigation actions in order for him to be able to arrive at the previously mentioned decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with our law, who was it who carried out investigations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Investigations were carried out by the investigative judges of the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the investigative judge in the position to decide on the proceedings, or in other words, what did the investigative judge do once the investigation was completed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: If I understood your question well, I believe that it consists of two parts. That's why I'm going to give you two answers. When the judge received the request to start proceedings, an investigation, the judge would evaluate this request and drafted an appropriate document by which he either allowed for the investigation to be carried out or rejecting such a request. In both cases the competent prosecutor's office had the right to appeal against such a decision and the final decision upon the appeal would be taken by the panel of judges of the competent court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would kindly ask you --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: After the end of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the second part of the question. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: After the end of the investigation, the investigative judge informed the competent prosecutor that the investigation was completed, and he forwarded to him the set of documents that resulted from the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, what is -- what kind of decision could be taken by the prosecutor once the investigation was completed and he was provided with the documents by the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: He could have taken three decisions. The first one would be to ask for additional investigation if he deemed that the investigation was not complete. Secondly, if he thought that the investigation was complete, he could take either of the two following decisions: Either to issue an indictment, or to halt any further proceedings, to suspend any further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, since you were a judge for a number of years, could you tell us whether there were situations, and if so, can you describe those situations to us, when judges became involved in certain investigations or although criminal proceedings had not been formally instigated.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there was such situations. And I can say that those situations were not uncommon. A common situation would be for an investigative judge to carry out certain activities before the criminal proceedings in the form of an on-site investigation, once he was informed that something had taken place which could later on be interpreted as a crime. The second situation is the situation in which the competent prosecution -- prosecutor could officially ask the competent investigative judge to carry out some preliminary actions that would serve -- that would help the prosecutor to decide whether official criminal proceedings would be started or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the judge carries out an on-site investigation upon having been informed that a crime might have been committed, who was it who was in charge of that investigation? Who was the one who decided how this on-site inspection or investigation would be carried out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: If this stage, the investigative judge is the absolute dominus litis. He is the one who decides what action will be taken and what course the investigation will take.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If an on-site investigation carried out by the judge also involves the police bodies, either the civilian or the military police, whose orders should they obey and what actions can they carry out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: An on-site investigation is carried out by the investigative judge. The investigative judge sets up a team and he requests from the police to place at his disposal certain experts with certain knowledge and certain equipment and then on site everything is carried out according to the judge's orders. During the on-site investigation, nobody can do anything that has not either been requested by the judge or approved by the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, when the investigative judge receives all the findings from the bodies from which he requested certain actions during the investigation, what does the judge do with all this material?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The evidence collected in this way is forwarded by the investigative judge to the competent prosecution, and in practice one copy is also forwarded to the police organs that were involved in the investigation, but this is not binding. It was just a custom. In any case, the answer to your question is that all the evidence is forwarded to the competent prosecutor, and at that moment the investigative judge, in terms of the court administration, concludes his case. He proclaims it completed, and it is filed in the court archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this procedural situation in which the investigative judge forwards the complete evidence to the prosecutor who is -- who takes over the management of the proceedings, who is it who decides how all the other involved actors will act? In other words, who decides that the evidence presents enough grounds for criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Again, the -- this is completely in the hands of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While the judge is conducting his on-site investigation, who is it who decides whether during the investigation certain professional or forensic activities will be carried out? Who is it who decides on the parts of procedure to be carried out in order to establish who the perpetrators of the possible crime were?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It is always and exclusively the investigative judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on to some other questions that arise from the documents, can you please tell me: When the judge who learns about the event does not have precise information as to where the event happened, who is it who decides whether an investigation will be carried out on site or, in other words, are there any real grounds for on-site inspection to be carried out in such a case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It is the investigative judge who decides on that. He will be the one to evaluate whether there are any grounds to conduct an on-site inspection if he learns that the on-site situation has changed, has been altered, that the evidence is no longer present there. So it is the investigative judge who has the right to decide on that. He makes a note of his decision, and this serves to complete this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Mr. Veseljak, to have a look at a document which is under number 1, and the number is DH276. Tell me first what kind of a document this is. Are you familiar with it or with the event? And who carried out the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I see from the signature that I wrote this document, which is a report on the investigation. Yes, I remember this event too. This was an event which was quite specific. It so happened that I was the on-duty investigating judge of the district military court. I happened to be an eyewitness of the event. And then I also carried out the on-site inspection -- investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This example of an on-site investigation report, could you tell us on the basis of it what are the elements that it has to contain and that have to be entered by the judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The on-site investigation report, as can be seen from this document, contains the markings, the number, the name of the court, the title, that it is an on-site investigation report. Then the team of investigators who carried out the actions required during the investigation. The main elements that the judge is -- was aware of before the investigation and during the investigation, certain basic elements about the event, followed by a description of the scene, which, depending on the circumstances, may be more or less detailed; then the eyewitnesses are listed, as well as other persons who might be useful at a later stage as witnesses if proceedings are instituted; and finally, the investigating judge describes the measures he undertook and the instructions he gave during the investigation, documents he signed to the police, forensic experts, and other persons, in the aim of collecting or describing the evidence or traces that may have been found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this second chapter, "Description of the scene," and in Chapter 5, it says that "The scene was sketched and photographed in detail and that the sketch and photographs will be a component part of this report." Does this statement correspond to what you said a moment ago, that the judge on the scene is duty-bound to wait for the forensic reports which he has required and, once he receives them, he hands everything over to the prosecutor? Does this sentence reflect your testimony about the role of the on-site judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. My headphones. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. All the instructions I gave as an investigating judge which could not be completed during the on-site investigation itself, I will wait for those documents, make a collection of those documents, and then forward them to the prosecutor without entering into any analysis of the documents I received. So if I gave instructions for a sketch to be made, then I will attach the sketch made following my instructions by members of the crime technology department of the military or civilian police, depending on the period of time. The same applies to photo documents, traces of blood, forensic reports about firearms, and -- et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at page 3, paragraph 3 from the bottom, which says: "Taking statements from the perpetrators and witnesses was handed over by the judge to military police organs." Does the on-site judge give instructions to the military police as well as to what they should do?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the statements taken by the police, be they the military or the civilian police, what is the significance of those statements in the proceedings themselves? Could the judge use those statements as evidence, that is, the trial judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The President and Their Honours will forgive me, but I will tell them what our practice was and how we called these reports. We called them "holy water," which meant that they could do no harm and no good; therefore, statements taken by the police according to the Law on Criminal Procedure could not be used as evidence that could be relied on by the court. If I remember well, Article 79 obliged the investigating judge himself that statements of this kind given to the police should be separated from other documents, that they should be kept separate from other documents. If the investigating judge omits to do this, there was a provision of Rule 323 which obliged the trial chamber to do the same, and in that case the trial chamber was duty-bound to return those separated documents to the investigating judge to keep separately from others, which meant these statements could not physically be part of the file, not to mention that they could not be used at trial. Should it so happen that the trial chamber used any one of these statements and relied on them for their judgement, this would mean an absolute violation of the criminal procedure and the higher level court would annul the decision of the lower court on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please now look at document under tab 2 and tell me whether this report is familiar and who did the investigation in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this report. I was the one who carried out the on-site investigation in this case. This case was unfortunately the worst case of civilian casualties in the town in which I live.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 2, please, "Steps taken." In paragraph 2 it says that "The duty judge allowed TV crews, Zetel, and BH Television to film the scene." Tell me, apart from actions required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] Yes ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, as it happens, this exhibit was discussed by the witness during the -- the Blaskic trial, and it's part of the documents I had prepared for cross-examination, so I do have a English translation, if Your Honours, you know, would like to -- to see the -- it will be ready. It's entirely up to you and, of course, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that the Defence was questioning the witness about document 2, and document 2 does have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thanks to our colleagues from the Prosecution, they provided us with documents they intend to use and they provided this document in English. In the meantime, we copied it and used that translation and provided copies for the Trial Chamber and for the other party. So thanks to this cooperation, we were able to have the document in translation. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Colleague Veseljak, I was just asking you about paragraph 2, under "Steps taken," when you approved or allowed --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. At least in the binder we received - and I take it the Judges have the -- the same one - there is no translation. So I do have my translation, but perhaps the Judges don't have it. I'm sorry to raise it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, you didn't give the translation to the Prosecution, but they have it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as following your suggestions we do our best to provide our colleagues far ahead of the time that we give them to you, so we apologise for not providing the translation in their binder, because we received the translation later. We did, however, provide the translation in the other binders, so everyone else does have a translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, tell me now, looking at this second paragraph under the subtitle "Steps taken," who has the competence during an investigation to allow others and not just the participants in the investigation the possibility of access to the scene or engaging in any other activities in -- in the area where the judge is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Whatever is happening on site, in those days there was a police ribbon. In those days -- nowadays we have these ribbons. In those days we didn't. But within the secure scene, the sovereign decision-maker is the investigating judge. Whatever is being done there, including who will be inside that secured area, which we call "the scene."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that the judge attaches all the evidence and documents that he collects -- he forwards that without looking into those reports. However, if the judge does give some sort of an assessment during the investigation, is it binding for the prosecutor and does the prosecutor have to take it as it is, as it stands?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The prosecutor is not bound by anything written by the investigating judge in his report. He takes a position about the contents, regardless of any assessments the report may contain. The investigating judge could make certain assessments to the effect that this could be used for further collecting evidence but later on it was the prosecutor who was the dominus litis who would decide about all the facts without being bound by the investigating judge or having to consult him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 3, where it says: "According to the greater characteristics, the investigating team came to the conclusion that the shells were fired from the Vitez-Bila direction." How did you come to this conclusion and was this one of the conclusions that was merely your own and was not binding for the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: You see, in any situation in life, one does acquire certain experience. We, unfortunately, learnt that a shell explosion leaves a very -- highly recognisable trace. If a shell were to come into contact with the surface at an angle of 90 degrees, then the dispersion of its shrapnel would take lines that would spread out equally from the centre in the form of a fan. However, shells usually hit the surface at a certain angle which is smaller than 90 degrees, and in those cases, as in this particular case, on the asphalt we have a visible spot in the form -- in the shape of a crater showing that the shell hit the surface at an angle and we know exactly where its point was, and in front of the shell there is a spread of the shrapnel in shorter lines; whereas, behind the lines the shrapnel disperse in longer lines. When you step at the point of contact and face opposite the point from which it came, you will see something, and what we saw was the direction west-southwest, and at the end of that imaginary line would be Vitez and Bila. Signing this report, I did not indicate the place from where the shell was fired but only the direction from which they came. So theoretically they could have come from the first department building in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, will you please look at document under tab 4, and tell me, please, what is the difference between this document entitled "Official report" in relation to the documents that you saw a moment ago that were entitled "On-site investigation report"? But first tell me: Do you recognize this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I do. I do recognise this document. The difference between an official report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Again, if the Defence could indicate for existing exhibits the number of the exhibit. It's easier for all the participants, including the clerks of the judges, you know, to trace the exhibit. And I think this one, if I correctly see, that's tab 4, which will be DH280. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Defence could tell us the exhibit number, if they have already become exhibits, for the benefit of the transcript and the other parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will correct my mistake. The previous document that Mr. Veseljak has commented on was a document of the district military court in Zenica, number 146 through 93, dated the 19th of April, 1993. This document is DH280.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Veseljak, will you please look at it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I already said that I do recognise this document. The difference between this official report and an on-site investigation report is the following: This time again we went to carry out the on-site investigation. That was our intention. Upon arriving close to the scene, we learnt that the scene had been changed, the bodies of the victims had been taken away, that the on-site situation had changed, that we are in the area of direct war operations, and the investigating judge came to the conclusion that there were no conditions or reason to carry out the investigation. And as can be seen, certain instructions were given, but we did not carry out the investigation itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of this official report entitled "Description of the crime scene," you said that the bodies had been taken to Dragovici village, that the traces had been destroyed, and the scene of the crime altered. For the on-site judge, is that reason enough for him to be unable to carry out an investigation on site and is prompted to make such a decision, or what decision could he later take in situations of this kind, as you have described?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I have to say first that the duty of the judge is not to carry out an investigation anywhere but on the crime scene, the actual scene of the event. The reason in this case for not carrying out the investigation is that the bodies had been taken away, which means that the on-site situation is not as it was initially. However, during further proceedings, should it prove to be essential for persons, objects, and the actual event to be located at a particular site, it is possible to reconstruct the scene as prescribed by the Law on Criminal Procedure and this is carried out by the court in keeping with the relevant rules. May I just add this does not mean posterior investigation. It means reconstructing the event, assuming how it took place, and this is done on the basis of certain other evidence, traces collected, forensic opinions, witness statements, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you look at document under tab 5, this reconstruction, when is it done? Is it done before or during the criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: If you ask me what the prevalent practice was, then this act is undertaken during criminal proceedings. But the same legal basis exists if the trial judge requires from the investigating judge a reconstruction. Both possibilities are envisaged, but it was more frequently done during the trial phase itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look now at document under tab 5. It is a document of the district military court of Zenica, number 202 through 93 dated the 1st of September 1993. Do you recognize this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document too is entitled "Official note." Look at the first paragraph after the investigation team is listed. Do we find here a similar situation as in the previous case leading to a similar decision on your part and wasn't this customary on the part of judges who found that the scene had been altered in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about a more or less identical situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at document under tab 6, entitled "CRY [as interpreted] 219 through 93 dated the 17th of October, 1993." Is that another document that you can recognise?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this document, we can see that there was a dilemma as to who the possible perpetrators of this act were. Tell me what you did in this case and is this one of the documents showing one of the ways in which the investigating judge acted in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this follows from your earlier questions about the division of competencies. The duty judge, the duty on-site judge of the military district court, in keeping with the competence of the court, did carry out on-site investigations; however, there were different situations, and I would like to remind you that the time in question was a time of war and that information that we received initially was very scarce and did not provide you with the ample grounds to decide what to do. And this is one of the situations in which I asked my colleague who was on duty at the time - he was a judge of the municipal court - I asked him to accompany me to the site and to try and see what happened and who of the two of us would be really competent in the case, and then once this was decided the competent person would complete the investigation, or in other words, his activities would end up with the investigation report and the activities of the other person would end up with an official note in which he would state that he was present and that he did take certain steps during the course of the activities. This document that you are showing to me now is somewhat specific because I was the duty judge at the time and I recognise some circumstances for which I thought that I should take interest in them because this situation involved some missing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, can you please look at the documents which are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. after tab 2, from 1 to 7. And for the record, I'm going to read their numbers. The first one is 1366. The second one is document of the -- dated 25 August 1993. Number 3 is document of the prosecutor's office of Zenica, KT387/93. The date is 25 August 1993. Number 4 is a document issued by the Zenica district military court. The number is KI243/93, dated 29 October 1993. Number 5 is document number 1560. Number 6 is document 1973. And finally, number 7 is a document issued by the Zenica senior public prosecutor's office, number KT11/94, dated 5 March 1994. My question to you is as follows: When you look at these documents, tell me, please, whether they are documents issued by the competent prosecutor's office by which the prosecutor requests an investigation to be carried out. In other words, are these documents of the investigating judge by which the investigations are allowed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, these are indeed such documents. I'm looking at the request, and based on the request there is a decision by which the investigative judge decides that an investigation will be carried out, and this document number KT389/83 [as interpreted], there is a mistake in the title. It says here "To the senior prosecutor," so this is not to the -- to the senior public prosecutor's office but from the senior public prosecutor's office. So this is a typo in the way you interpreted the title. So these are the documents, one preceding and one following. The preceding document is a request for investigation and the subsequent act is the decision of the judge by which it is stated that the investigation will indeed be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first document. In the description of the action, it says that "In the village of Bjelavici somebody took a cow weighing 280 kilogrammes from an abandoned Croatian house and a calf. After that, it says that this is an aggravated burglary from Article 148 of the Penal Code. My first question to you is as follows: Who would be the first body who would suggest a certain legal qualification of the crime that is the subject of the criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It is the competent prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. If -- perhaps I am the only one who can't follow. But just, again, identify which document are we now talking about. She says it's the first document. And I looked at it and this one dates 5th August 1993, a B/C/S document. It carries the Defence number 1366. Is that the one we are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, could you please be more precise and can you tell us whether this document is, after tab 2 in the binder, chapter number 2, and the date is 5th August 1993? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the document, and the number is 1366. My question to the witness is as follows:

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Firstly, is this a request to carry out an investigation which is the beginning of every criminal proceedings? And the witness confirmed that. And now I have asked the witness to comment upon the description of the event, after the name of Jakob Torsum [phoen], in paragraph 3, and in which the event or part of the event is described as I have quoted it, and there is also the legal qualification of this crime, and it says here that this is an aggravated theft pursuant to Article 148. My question to the witness was: What is the first or the primary body that suggests what the qualification of the crime should be, the crime that is the subject of this criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The witness started his answer by saying that the first body that suggests the legal qualification of the crime is the prosecutor's office that files the request for criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, who is it who decides on the final qualification -- legal qualification of the crime? In other words, is the court duty-bound to adopt the qualification proposed by the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The court is not bound by that legal qualification, and the final decision on the legal qualification of the crime lies with the court and only the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when it comes to the police, did the police have any say whatsoever in the factual description and the legal qualification of the crime as proposed by the prosecutor, or can they have a say in the final qualification of the crime as decided upon by the court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The police has no obligation whatsoever to suggest any qualification, legal qualification of the crime. In practice, it does happen that the police try to see what a crime could constitute in legal terms. However, this suggestion is not binding on -- either upon the prosecutor or the court. So in other words, the police does not have any say whatsoever as to what the legal qualification of the crime would be in the further proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the description of this crime that I have just quoted, it says that some things were stolen from the abandoned houses of Croat citizens. Tell me, please: How did you as a judge evaluate and assess such acts? How did you qualify those acts during your tour of duty in the military district court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I did that from the point of view of the factual description of the crime as per the Code. We evaluated whether in the actions perpetrated by a person we could find the elements of crime in the way this crime is described in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Penal Code, which was in effect at the time, which was the Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia, which was later on adopted by Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are also crimes against the civilian population that were committed during the war and one element of those crimes is also theft and plunder. Tell me, please: Did you in the court find any elements or did you have any elements that could serve as the base for qualifying such and similar acts in keeping with the provisions of the Penal Code?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: In a similar way, in the way that the court was not bound by the qualification of the crime, it was bound by the fact provided to him by the prosecutor about the crime that he was in charge of. Obviously in every crime that happens during the war you are bound to recognise possible murders of the crime -- war crime against the civilian population pursuant to the then-provision 142 of the Penal Code. However, in this particular case, these things were done by thief -- before the war, during the war. Unfortunately, it is still being done by thieves today. So whenever you have such a factual description, you will not find any elements to qualify such crimes as war crimes. We -- and when I say "we," I don't want to speak on behalf of the others, so I'd like to say I was 14 thinking whether I could recognise a certain intention to perpetrate war crimes or it was just the case of somebody needing a cow and the easiest thing for this perpetrator to do was to go to an abandoned house and steal a cow from such an abandoned house. I have also to say that very soon there were no -- there was no longer abandoned property and thieves continued stealing cows.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, were such crimes committed also against other ethnic groups or did the situation apply only to one ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: These crimes involved those who possessed a cow. Unfortunately, the situation was horrendous, and some people made the most of that horrendous situation in order to steal goods from whoever the goods belonged to. If we embarked on a statistical analysis, you -- we will notice that at a certain moment the victims of the crimes were more often members of a different ethnic group in a village that had been abandoned by -- by the population. However, that statistic will soon change because there were no more abandoned cattle after a while and theft continued. So if you look at the final statistical picture, you will see that the victims of the crime were members of -- of our own ethnic group, rather than of a different ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you evaluated crimes as a judge, can you tell me whether the legislator, on the one hand, and the army or the 3rd Corps, on the other hand, tried and did they do everything possible in order to prevent such crime? Did they ask for efficient prosecution or did such -- was such practice tolerated in the area?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Let me start by answering the second part of your question first. No, this was not tolerated, and I can illustrate that by giving you an example. I personally during the 39 months of the existence of the military court, either as an individual judge or a member of a panel, I was sitting in over 750 cases. I was involved in over 250 criminal proceedings. I believe that these figures speak for themselves, and this equally applies to all the other colleagues of mine. There were an average of eight of us during that period of time. In addition to that, I know the following: The military authorities in some participants of the territory which were very sensitive because they were populated by the minority population who were sometimes exposed to harassment by individuals and who by the logic of the matter felt more exposed -- so the military set up checkup points in order to prevent looting of property from these areas. And I assure you that every perpetrator who could be detected was prosecuted by the competent bodies. The police would report them and then the prosecutors would prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, do you remember before the war what was the penalty for aggravated theft as provided for by the law?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I can't be 100 per cent sure that I remember, but I believe that it was a maximum of five years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, do you know what was the penalty for theft of property from an abandoned house?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I remember. It was either ten years or a maximum, it could have been capital punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the legislator and the bodies that were involved in investigation of looting from abandoned property? Was the position that this was a lesser crime or a crime equal to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. For the cases of aggravated robbery and aggravated theft and the crimes of war crimes against the civilian population, the punishment was identical in terms of a special minimum, a special maximum, and in terms of the penalty provided for by the law. It was from ten years in prison up to the capital punishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I complete my examination, I should just like to ask you to look at tab 4, and from 1 -- or Chapter 4, from 1 to 16, entitled "Judgements," and could you please recognise the judgements that you personally handed down or were a member of a trial chamber that handed them down during the war as a member of the military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I seem to be having problems like the prosecutor. You are referring to Chapter 4 "Judgements"? And the first judgement is dated K12/93? Is that the one you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Look at number 7, which is number IK233/93, dated the 27th of September, 1993. Tell me, is this a judgement that you handed down as president of a trial chamber? Would you be kind enough to look at the document under tab 11, with the number Zenica district military court number IK334/94, dated the 8th of September, 1995. Do you recognize this judgement too?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I recognise this one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a judgement for aggravated robbery provided for by the Criminal Code, Rule 151/2. Was that the crime you referred to a moment ago for which the same penalty was provided as for the crime of war crime against civilian -- the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But one correction: In this case, Mehrid Duvnjak [phoen], when committing the crime, was a young adult, and that is why he could not be sentenced to death but in principle the answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Veseljak, who decided about the penalty itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The trial chamber, consisting of five members: Two professional judges and three lay judges, had a total of five votes. So each one of them had one vote, and the majority would decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document under tab 12, it is Zenica district military court number IK552/94 dated the 9th of December, 1994. It of course refers to events in 1993. Tell me, did you participate in rendering this decision?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the trial chamber in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document number 13, district military court number IK606 through 94 from the 21st of December, 1994, is this a judgement that you were involved in as a judge of the district military court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
