utterances.text: Yes, in this case as president of the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at document number 14. It is the document of the Zenica court, IK169/93, dated the 13th of June, 1995. Were you involved in this case as a judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, and again, as the presiding judge. But if I may, I would like to say why I emphasised when I was the presiding judge and when I was a member of the trial chamber. The Law on Criminal Procedure prescribed the order in which judges would participate in chambers. When I was the presiding judge, I would have the last vote when it came to the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The previous document was DH314, and this document we are talking about is DH155/20. So a moment ago you said you were a member of the chamber, and with respect to this one, of the 13th of June, you were the presiding judge. Now, please look at the next two documents of the Zenica high court, number K194/96, dated the 20th of March, 1997. Tell us, were you a judge in this case? And the document under number 16, K67/00, dated the 12th of March, 2002. Tell me whether this was a case that you tried.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: In this one, I was the presiding judge, and the witness who is following me was a member of the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, in these several cases, we saw that the sentences were handed down in 1994, 1995, and even after the war. Can you tell us briefly the kind of problems you encountered in discovering, prosecuting, and sentencing -- you were faced with, especially the courts, and why in some cases the proceedings lasted some time. Actually, my first question would be whether proceedings were conducted speedily or not; and an additional question: Why did in some cases trials last a long time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Let me say first of all that in my deep conviction, trials did not take long but what did take long was the preliminary process before a trial could start. There were problems with communications. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The last document you showed me, I was then already a judge of the cantonal court, because this took place in 2002. There were very great problems in finding people, identifying people. The territory was cut up and it was impossible to communicate between various areas. The event that this last document refers to took place in Bugojno or Gornji Vakuf, which means that between the territory covered by the district military court and this area was the area of another warring party which couldn't be crossed. People moved around without ID documents. I will give you an example, with your permission: At the cantonal court much later, we tried a murder in which a man, an Egyptian citizen, was allegedly murdered. His name was Hisham Diyab and we found the man guilty and sentenced him for this crime. Several years later, through the mediation of the Egyptian Embassy, Mr. Hisham Diyab appeared. He is well, alive, and kicking, thank God, a doctor in Egypt. So it just shows the circumstances under which we worked and how we strove to be efficient. But we had enormous difficulties of an objective nature, not due to any -- any lack of will on the part of the court. I have to tell you that never in my life and never again in my life will I work as hard as I did in this period of time we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Veseljak, as judges or the prosecutor in your courts or the police, be it civilian or military, could they from January 1st, 1993 until the end of the war reach areas that were de facto under the control of the HVO or the VRS to investigate an event, to find a witness, to interview a witness? Did you have any such possibilities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: With the exception of murder, no -- I'm sorry, with the exception of suicide, no [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Mr. Veseljak, now: Mr. Veseljak, as a person who spent the whole time in the district military court from the moment it was founded until it ceased to operate, when looking back at that period and your work in the court and the policy of the 3rd Corps to prevent, detect, and punish the perpetrators of all crimes, do you believe now that more could have been done than all of you together managed to do, that is, the military authorities, the prosecutors, and the judges? Could you have done more than you actually did?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: If you're asking me and in view of the circumstances under which we worked, we could not have done more. If I look back today, fortunately some wounds have healed over the years and I'm doing my best to forget many of the things that happened. But when you make me look back, as you are doing now, I wonder from this point of view how we managed to do as much as we did, because during 39 months I signed 750 judgements, three and a half thousand cases were processed at the district military court. I believe several thousand - I'm not quite sure of the figure - several thousand requests for investigations, endless decisions on detention on remand, innumerable instances when witnesses got killed, when they left to go to third countries, we couldn't trace them. In a situation when a single photograph with a camera was something we could only dream about, when the paraffin glove test was something from outer space because you simply didn't have paraffin, when we had to run to the laboratory to take blood traces because we didn't have any means to prevent coagulation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes our examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I close this now? Oh, it's not finished. I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, the other Defence team, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it will be best to have the break straight away, and we will resume at about 6.00 and give the floor to the Prosecutor for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to the Prosecution, and don't forget that we are supposed to finish at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Judges will also need a few minutes for their questions. And so if you take too long, we will have to continue tomorrow, tomorrow morning. In any case, you will be given the same time as the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. If the -- Your Honours and the Defence could be distributed a set of documents which I intend to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just start with just a few general points about the role of a duty judge. And I believe you were a duty judge, a judge quite a number of times, you know, in 1992 and 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think in the Blaskic case you also said that a duty judge was on shift. He was available, I think, for a week or so and would be called whenever it was required to do so.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who would assign judges -- duty judges to be on a certain shift? Who would do that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The president of the court, and there would be a rota. Every week we would start at 00 on Sunday and we finished at 2400 on the following Sunday, and we took turns. If there were eight of us and I had my shift during week 1, then my turn would again come during week 9, after all of my eight colleagues had their turns. And this was the only criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So in Zenica and for the jurisdiction of the military courts, there was one duty judge at one time.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, at any given time, there was a duty judge who was accompanied by a deputy of the district military prosecutor. I believe that in the prosecution their shifts were somewhat longer because there were fewer of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were called to a given case, one of these many, many you testified about before the break, how long on average would you be concerned with one of these cases, you as the duty judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It's hard to say for how long, but I can give you a description. For as long as it took me to complete my investigation and draft either an official note or an official record after that. So as soon as I completed my documentation and forwarded it to the competent prosecutor, I would be finished with the case. We tried to spend as little time as possible on the case, and I'm talking about the complete procedure. The on-site inspection itself took as long as it had to take, depending on what you found on the site, how many traces you had to collect, how big the site was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at a few of these documents which were presented to us, and it's amazing how quick you acted that -- when the events occurred on one day, usually the judge would arrive on the same day, and the report would carry the date of the next day. So it was a very, very efficient procedure.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: If you are talking about the records that I drew up, I have to say that the judgements that I signed as the presiding judge, I tried to dictate them on the following day. If you're asking me about on-site inspections, I can tell you that we arrived at the scene as fast as possible, as fast as this was doable. I arrived at a number of such scenes on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned a few documents, you know, which perhaps may be the result of your inquest as a duty judge. Would it be correct to say that the typical document, report which comes out of a detail for you as a duty judge was this on-site inspection report? That would be a typical work product of you being called as a duty judge to a crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, on a condition that an on-site inspection was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And if it wasn't carried out, you would even include that very fact, as you have testified before the break, into the report, that it was not possible to go to a specific crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you already talked about a few of these reports, and I -- I'm going through a few of them again. But let me start with a different one. And this one is contained in tab 1. That's the first document. It's a Defence exhibit, DH279, and it has been discussed here before Your Honours with Judge Adamovic. And I would just like you to have a look at this report. It dates 23rd July 1993 and is a on-site investigation report. Now, that's again a typical report: Two pages, very succinct, a typical example of -- of an on-site investigation report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Please give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Please take -- take your time. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Let us say that this is a typical report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we see that Mr. Adamovic went to the -- to the crime scene and he looked at what -- what happened. Apparently here a person was killed while a -- a weapon was being cleaned, a person called Asim Sivro was cleaning that weapon. And Mr. Adamovic was very precise in the location he found the body of the victim. I think he says the body was sort of half-sitting position, back to the wall. And he also looked at blood traces. Now, let me ask you: How important is it to record exactly the position of a victim, a body, in your assessment? And you have a lot of experience.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Whenever this is possible for the subsequent actions, this is what one should do. This is important in principle; however, one cannot be as precise as my colleague Adamovic was in this particular case. If one takes this as being very precise, one cannot always be as precise as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But certainly the aim has to be as precise as possible under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: No objection to that. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, another feature we see here is the heading "Information about the participants," and Mr. Adamovic -- our colleague talked about, you know, witnesses, mentioned specifically names of witnesses, and I believe these are army members. And again, my -- my question is: How important is it to list witnesses who may have been eyewitnesses to the events, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: This is very important, if such information is available. If you make an effort and if you look at the records that I signed, you will see that I had an identical approach. Whenever I had information about participants or eyewitnesses, I would make a record of that. If we didn't know that, then we would instruct the military police to continue with their operative work in order to get as much information as possible about possible participants in the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we see that on the second page of the English translation. It may be also on the second page -- on the first one in your original, the role of the military police. But let me go to the penultimate paragraph, when he talks about information of relatives, and then, I quote, "As well as the command of the brigade to which the person who inflicted the injury and the injured person belonged." Perhaps you can tell us, how important is it to inform, you know, these people, the relatives, and here the brigade? If you can help us.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: First I have to tell you that this is certainly not a job of the investigative judge. However, beyond this context, I would also provide information if I had an opportunity to learn where they are and if I were in the position to provide such information. However, these are personal reasons, not formal reasons. This is what military police anywhere in the world in the course of events should certainly do. They should do it, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last paragraph talks about the vicinity of combat operations and that the scene of the crime was very close to -- to the front line. I believe you also were working under difficult conditions in your work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Most often, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we might come to that, to the Zenica shelling of the 19th of April, 1993. I think there you even conducted your investigation as a duty judge while detonations were still being heard. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I do remember that. At that time, I was involved in an on-site inspection. I was not in charge of investigations. I was involved in a very concrete investigative action. I was involved in an on-site inspection while detonations could be heard. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe occasionally on the 19th of April you had even to take shelter because, you know, you -- you feared, and rightly so, for your life and the life of the people who were with you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on to the next document, and this is tab 3 in this bundle, and this is a document which features you as the duty judge. Just take a look at the whole document, if you may. It's DH278, a Defence exhibit, an on-site investigation report dated 1st of June, 1993. And if you have familiarised yourself, do you still remember this investigation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, first of all, just above the title "Description of crime scene," I see the sentence: "The scene of crime was secured by members of the Military Police Battalion." That would be a battalion of the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was that a normal feature that you would ask the military police to secure a -- a area? You talked about in your chief that at that time you didn't have these red-white tapes, if I correctly remember. But at that time, did you sort of always have the military police operating on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Let me first tell you something about this particular event. In this particular event that we are discussing now, members of the military police battalion secured the scene of crime because they were deployed in its vicinity. This is what I said in the course of my direct. There was a checkpoint the role of which was to protect the Croatian population in the Stranjani village and that's why they were first to arrive at the scene of crime. The military police was always involved in the investigations -- actually, the police. Sometimes the military police, sometimes the civilian police. Everything that we did was assisted by the military police; to be more specific, by the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps. There were also some exceptions. There were some situations when I asked for the assistance of the civilian police because the event was of such a nature that I required a more professional team of crime experts, a team that was better equipped with equipment and everything that was necessary to carry out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, on the first page of this report, under the title "Description of crime scene," you talk about - assuming you, I mean you drafted this report - you talk about, and I quote, "Traces of blood and a bloody bandage were found at about 10 metres away in the direction of the woods and a gate was found next to the cow. The trace of a bullet was found on a tree trunk on the edges of this clearing and about 5 metres away there were several traces where the bullets struck on the ground." And then you talk about photographs and sketches and so on. Now, how important is it to look for traces of bullets and -- and properly describe it in a -- in such a report, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I believe that this is extremely important. No doubts about that. And every time you are in a position to do that, you should do that. It is better to collect everything at the scene, even if it is not important and even if later on you discover that those things are not important, than to leave something uncollected. If you're asking me in principle, this would -- this would be my answer to you. In this particular case, whatever I was able to locate, I collected. It was easy to collect evidence because the area was peaceful, it was secure, and I had ample time to collect all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the incident itself. The way I understand it and it is described under the heading "Probable course of events," was that initially a cow was stolen, abducted, and this incident, the stealing of a cow - and you've mentioned cows before the break, by the way, on a couple of incidents - triggered two members of the military police to get involved. So being Swiss, I have obviously no problem with taking cows very seriously, but why is it -- was it such an importance to investigate using military police resources for that? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: You don't understand. Your cows are violet and they have a name; they're called Milka, aren't they? But here we're talking about a different thing, we're talking about an area in which there is a certain number of Croats residing and during the conflict they did not leave their homes. And one of them had his cow stolen. He informed two military policemen at the checkpoint that this had happened. This checkpoint had been set up in order to protect this particular population from such incidents, from somebody stealing their cow. These two military policemen decided that they could not intervene on their own. In the meantime, the thieves took a cow to a place which you could call a thicket or a wood and this is where they slaughtered the cow, because I believe that they deemed that they -- it would be easy for them to cover the traces of the theft if they slaughtered the cow and butchered it. When these two military policemen got reinforcements, they encircled the area where these two thieves were with the butchered cow, with the beheaded cow, and they asked them to surrender. Fire was opened. The military police returned fire. And the result was what it was. And you can see what happened from the reports. One of -- one of the military policemen succumbed to his wounds. The other one was seriously injured but -- but survived. And that is why the intervention of the military police was needed. The military police intervened in order to detect and capture the perpetrators of this serious crime. I must say that during the time when this crime was committed, the -- the penalty envisaged for this crime was a minimum of five years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you would agree that a lot of resources and efforts, even fighting, you know, shooting, was involved in -- in arresting the two alleged perpetrators of that stealing of the cow.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I don't know what you are trying to imply. In my view, we -- we reacted with an adequate response. At that particular moment, I'm sure that none of the policemen intended to shoot at the perpetrators. However, if you're a policeman and if you see somebody fleeing, if you ask them to surrender and they open fire at you, I don't know whether you would say that the reaction was inadequate and that this should not have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe here, again, witnesses were traced and -- and talked to in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I have to change my glasses now. I can't see you very well with my reading glasses, and with the others I can't read. I think you're right, but let me look. I know that at the time we knew about the policemen. I remember that. But I don't believe that we knew at the time the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but I think later you found out that there were two persons called Fetic and then I believe you included that into this report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, that's important that the -- obviously the possible perpetrators are named right from the beginning if -- if they are known or can be ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: There's -- also exists a criminal report against an unknown perpetrator, and as a lawyer I think it is very important to document an event, even if you don't know who the perpetrators are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go to the next exhibit. That's tab 4. Again, it's a Defence exhibit, DH280. And you have talked about that before the break, because my learned colleague has showed you this document already. Just a couple of points. It's about the killing of four persons in a village called Sastavci on the 18th of August, 1993, and apparently that village -- the municipality, Vares, lies, and I quote your report,"in the zone of war operations." And again, here you obviously didn't achieve to go to the crime scene, and it's reported in -- under item 1, "Description of the crime scene," that you could not go there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yet you were able - and that's on page 2 of the English translation and I believe also in your B/C/S version under item 3 - there were some witnesses available who were talked to perhaps not by you but by somebody else, and you incorporated that information into your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: That is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And specifically, the second person, the witness B, Ibrahim Sarac, the commander of the Bosnian Independent Company - I'll just read out the first sentence of the what he apparently took - "a few hours after we took over duty in our zone of responsibility, one villager informed us that four bodies were lying on the road leading to Dragovici village not far from Ljesvaca [phoen] village." He goes on and says what he was doing. How important, again in your assessment, having dealt with all these military units on the ground, was it to talk to the commander who was there and who could give information about what was happening in his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I understood correctly your question, so would you be kind enough to elaborate a little. I didn't quite understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry for the unprecise question. You see that apparently you had information about two witnesses or the person who drafted the report; that was your colleague Mr. Armin Seco. The first witness was a -- in fact, two witnesses, Fikret Krivokapa and Fahrudin Krivokapa, two members of the SJB police forces, that's under A. And then you also had information from a Mr. Ibrahim Sarac. He was the commander of the Bosnian Independent Company, the unit in whose area of operations or the zone of responsibility the crimes occurred. My question is for you: As duty judge, how important is it to talk to the military commander of a unit who was in the vicinity and perhaps indeed in the middle of that area where the crime scene was lying.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I don't believe that it was of any special importance; however, you can see that my very young colleague at the time, Armin Seco and myself were in a situation where we learnt that the bodies had been taken from the scene, that we were on the edge of the area of combat operations, and on that occasion we wanted to learn from peoples who were not eyewitnesses of the event but who were witnesses of the consequences what we might see if we were able to enter that area, and we learnt that locals, villages, had removed the bodies, that they had informed the soldiers present that they had removed the bodies, that in passing they had seen pools of blood in the grass. These were elements that we wanted to find out about so as to collect as much information as possible and to be able to convey that information to the prosecutor later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So to summarise, because you did not have access to the crime scene, you tried to talk to people who could sort of give information about the -- the vicinity and the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Certain information, assuming that they knew something which might give us indication as to where we should look for future -- in our future investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on to the next exhibit, Mr. Veseljak, and that's tab 5, and again that's a document whose exhibit number is DH276, which you have discussed in -- in chief already. And you remember that's the one dating 26 December 1992 to which you were also a witness, an eyewitness, the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, I see a very detailed description of the crime scene. It talks in the middle of the first paragraph about a ricochet, a bullet which had hit the radiator of a Golf car, and so on. So again, that would be an example of what's requested if somebody like a duty judge or indeed the police goes to a crime scene where a murder or a -- a murder involving the death of a person is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: All I can do is agree with what you said. You haven't asked me anything yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. On the next page, you even went -- the next page in the English version and I think in your version it's the same -- you are very detailed again about the calibres of a gun. You talk about the locations where a cartridge was found. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Something I'm interested in is the following: After you talk about eyewitnesses to this incident and just above the heading "Measures taken," we see that - and I quote the paragraph - "Along with the injured man, the MUP employee also tried to arrest Sead Patkovic, son of Serif, residing in Nemila, one Ahmet Spahica number 6 who was probably also an eyewitness to the entire incident." Do you remember that? It's sort of unusual that an eyewitness needs to be arrested in order to provide his account for what has happened. Perhaps you remember what this was all about. Just above the heading "Measures taken."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the spot you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's on page 2 of your B/C/S version, the last paragraph, "Zajedno," and so on. Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm trying to recollect the whole event, to reconstruct it in my memory. It was the centre of town, the street lined with houses on both sides, and in those days at that spot people were illegally converting money for German marks, and everything started with a police raid against these people who were converting foreign currency for local currency. So what you're reading out to me, I wouldn't call it "arrest." It is a normal police procedure whereby an eyewitness is identified and asked for an interview, an informative interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that once again we have a problem with the translation. I am looking at the English translation, which says "arrest." And in our own language, it says "to take in." And that -- or "bring in." So that may be the cause of some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... obviously controlling what the B/C/S version says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Anyway, do you remember the person Sead Patkovic, son of Serif? Do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know his father -- what appears to be his father, Serif Patkovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I don't know who the person named Serif Patkovic may be. But since I know what it is you're leading up to, I know that there is a Serif Patkovic. I assure you that this person who was a very young man could not have been -- had a son of the age that would be of interest for the police. You see, we have villages with the entire population bearing the same surname and every other person having the same first name. You know, father Serif, son Serif. These are local customs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to the -- to the next page, the last page of this document. And, first of all, it mentions an interesting -- item 4 says: "The perpetrator underwent a paraffin test." So I take it that, you know, when you said before the break that it was -- I don't know what the exact words you used -- impossible or it would have been a miracle to have it. Occasionally it was done, a paraffin test.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: We did have paraffin for a time, so we did do the paraffin tests. And then later on we had no paraffin and we couldn't do the test. And I must say to you as a professional that for me as a professional I was not too sorry about the paraffin glove test because, as you know, by itself it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is not proof of anything. The reaction you get is non-specific, through nitrates, and it can only indirectly lead to gunpowder. When you have a pistol, an eyewitness, an admission, then the paraffin test may be of use. If you only have that test, then it's better not to have it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on to another paragraph on this page, and it's the third one from the bottom. It starts: "On 27th December 1992, an autopsy was performed. Attended by the judge and on this occasion a piece of lead bullet without its jacket was found in the left lobe of the cerebellum of the deceased, which was also handed over to VP operative Alija Limanovic." Again, for you as a duty judge, an investigative judge, how important is it to look for, find, report the presence of a bullet in -- in one of these bodies of a victim?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: I have to tell you something else first: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure in force at the time, it is the duty of the investigating judge, though this may seem strange to you now -- it was the legal obligation of the investigating judge to prepare a report on the postmortem. We found various ways to do this. We attended postmortems and copied down what the person performing the postmortem found during the autopsy. And if we ordered an autopsy, it was very important for me to find out the finding, because the finding of the autopsy was an indication of many other things that may later arise during the investigation: The type of weapon, the direction, the angle of the projectile, the injuries caused, the injuries that were the cause of death, et cetera. So in answer to your question, it was very important to write down what the autopsy produced as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: A related issue is the firearms, you know, the object of -- one of the objects, you know, which -- which may be helpful in finding what has occurred. Can you confirm that you as, you know, the representative of the authority had the power to seize firearms of alleged perpetrators and to analyse them in order to establish which rifle has fired, which empty shells match with the rifles found, and -- and so on? You had the authority to do that and you -- you did that? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In this particular case, as you have chosen this one, which is highly specific -- you see, it was up to my personal assessment. Due to the highly tense situation that all this was happening under, I seized a cocked pistol from the man's hand. Now, whether I had the authority, it's up to you to judge, but that is what I actually did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Because you wanted to find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The actual act of seizing the pistol from his hand was simply motivated by stopping further action. This seizure of the pistol, which I ordered the police to do against a receipt on temporary seizure, was intended for further criminal processing to establish that the bullets that we found had come from the -- that weapon, that the jackets we found had been fired with that weapon. You're familiar with the technique. I don't want to waste your time explaining how we compared disputed and undisputed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go on to -- briefly only to the Zenica shelling of the 19th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's -- the report is in tab 2 of my -- my bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You already talked about that, and you were certainly very specific also in the -- in the Blaskic trial about that. Just a couple of points: In the Blaskic trial, you were shown and commented upon a number of documents -- a number of photographs from the crime scene and you explained, you know, the craters, whatever you also told us before the break. Now, again in your expertise as a judge, an investigative judge, how important is it to take photographs of the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: It is of fundamental importance. In this particular case, I have to tell you that we made as many photographs as we had available film.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a couple of other points about the Zenica shelling of the 19th April. Just to confirm: It was you who ordered the civil defence people to clean, to wash, the area from -- from blood? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: The next day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just to go back to -- to the previous point: It was you who had ordered the people, the specialist technicians, to take the photos of all these impacts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be best to stop now. We will continue tomorrow, because you haven't exhausted the time available to you and the Defence will certainly have some re-examination, as will the Judges. So, sir, unfortunately you will have to stay until tomorrow, so I would like to ask you to come for the hearing which will begin tomorrow morning, luckily for you, because often we work in the afternoon. But tomorrow we will continue at 9.00, and the Witness and Victims Department will make sure that you will be present here tomorrow at 9.00. From now until then, you must not meet with anyone because, as you have taken the solemn declaration, you're a witness of justice and you mustn't have any contact now with the Defence, which brought you here as a witness. I'm going to ask the usher to be kind enough to accompany you out of the courtroom, and we will see you again tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I've missed St. Valentines Day with my wife today, I can just as well stay tomorrow. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tomorrow we will continue our work, beginning at 9.00. How much more time do you need do you think? You haven't taken an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps 20 minutes, half an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. So we will now adjourn, and I'll see you all again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
